{{Views}}
[[File:Dodecahedron flat.svg|thumb|right|240px|Net of a [[dodecahedron]]. All edges in this net have true length.]]
In [[descriptive geometry]], '''true length''' is any distance between points that is not foreshortened by the view type.<ref>Manual of Engineering Drawing 2009, {{ISBN|0750689854}}, pp. 81–85</ref> In a three-dimensional [[Euclidean space]], lines with true length are [[parallel (geometry)|parallel]] to the [[projection plane]]. For example, in a top view of a [[Pyramid (geometry)|pyramid]], which is an [[orthographic projection (geometry)|orthographic projection]], the [[base (geometry)|base]] [[edge (geometry)|edges]] (which are parallel to the projection plane) have true length, whereas the remaining edges in this view are not true lengths. The same is true with an orthographic [[side view]] of a pyramid. If any face of a pyramid was parallel to the [[projection plane]] (for a particular view), all edges would demonstrate true length.

Examples of views in which all edges have true length are [[net (polyhedron)|nets]].
